title: Largest Rectangle in Histogram
statement: Given bar heights in `heights` (each bar width is 1), return the area of the largest rectangle that can be formed in the histogram.

predict_steps.prompt: Bars 5 and 6 form height 5 width 2. What area?
When a shorter bar arrives, what happens to taller indices on the stack?

reference_solution:
def largest_rectangle(heights):
    heights = list(heights) + [0]
    stack = [-1]
    best = 0
    for i, h in enumerate(heights):
        while stack[-1] != -1 and heights[stack[-1]] > h:
            height = heights[stack.pop()]
            width = i - stack[-1] - 1
            best = max(best, height * width)
        stack.append(i)
    return best

viva.question: Why does a monotonic stack find the largest rectangle in linear time?
expected_points: each bar index is pushed once and popped at most once
a shorter bar to the right closes the width of taller waiting bars
area is computed when a bar is popped using the new left and right bounds
amortized work across all bars stays linear

viva.question: What is the largest rectangle for a single bar or for all equal heights?
expected_points: a single bar has area equal to its own height
n equal bars form a rectangle of height times n
draining the stack at the end with a zero sentinel forces those areas to be counted
forgetting the sentinel leaves the final increasing run unprocessed

viva.question: Why does a smaller bar to the right bound the width of taller bars?
expected_points: a rectangle of tall height cannot extend past a shorter neighbor
the popped bar's right boundary is the current index
its left boundary is the new stack top after the pop
those bounds are exactly where the height remains at least that bar's height
